newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Frosty start to Zaire peace talks as rebels advance.
newsitem.headline: Frosty start to Zaire peace talks as rebels advance.

text.p: The government of Zaire and rebel forces bent on toppling President Mobutu Sese Seko began peace talks in South Africa on Saturday as the rebel army captured another key city.

News of the fall of Mbuji-Mayi, a diamond mining centre in central Zaire, came as foreign minister Kamanda wa Kamanda and the chief representative of Laurent Kabila's rebel alliance, Bizima Karaha, exchanged an icy handshake in Pretoria at the start of formal negotiations.

Kabila's Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (AFDL), now threatening to capture Zaire's second largest city, Lubumbashi, were clearly negotiating from a position of strength.
Mobutu's negotiating team now includes representatives of a government under the leadership of one of his main rivals, Etienne Tshisekede, as well as opposition party members.
Karaha's opening statement underlined the widespread view that rebel successes on the battlefield and Kabila's mounting popularity with the people had driven the government into negotiations.
"We are here because those brothers of ours have realised for the first time they can't make it with mercenaries and genociders. They can only make it with us if they still want to survive," he said.
"We asked for these negotiations more than five months ago. It is a good sign that (government negotiators) are here."
Kamanda and Mobuto's adviser Honore Ngbanda stared stonily ahead while the rebel envoy told them Zaire must be "free of misery, disease and dictatorship".
"That's why we are here," he said.
The two sides met in the circular cabinet room of the South African government, separated by South African Deputy President Thabo Mbeki and United Nations envoy Mohamed Sahnoun.
Noting that both sides had mandates to take decisions, Mbeki said: "Hopefully that will allow us to move the process forward rapidly."

"I know we should have no illusions as to the ability of such meetings to produce spectacular results," Sahnoun told the conference, which included most of the Pretoria diplomatic corps. "But we shall leave no stone unturned."

Asked later about the rebel forces' latest prize, Karaha told reporters: "Taking Mbuji-Mayi is not important. What is important is that not only Mbuji-Mayi, (but) the whole country should be liberated."
He said the main issue at the talks would be the departure from office of Zaire's president of the past 31 years. "Mobutu has to go ... the sooner the better," he said.
Zaire's charge d'affaires in Pretoria Issa Ganda-E-Ndzea said the talks would go on as long as necessary to achieve a settlement.
"If reaching a solution takes one day, if it takes two days or one month, it doesn't matter. The problem is not the length of the talks. We must just start talking," he told Reuters.
Asked if there was optimism that the talks could accomplish a ceasefire and peaceful transition in Zaire, one diplomat shrugged and said: "Let's just say there's a hope."

Members of a group of curious German tourists outside the stately sandstone Union Buildings where the talks opened were more forthright. "A new broom sweeps clean, eh?" said one. "Looks like time for a change in Zaire."
